name: God as guarantor of the continuity of unperceived objects
plain_explanation: If things only exist while being perceived, a tree would seem to blink in and out of existence depending on whether anyone is looking at it. Berkeley's solution: God is always perceiving everything, everywhere, so objects have a continuous existence even when no human is looking.
precise_definition: To the objection that unobserved objects (e.g., a tree with no one in the quad) would cease to exist, Berkeley replies that 'God always perceives everything'; without God, physical objects 'would have a jerky life, suddenly leaping into being when we look at them,' but God's constant perception secures their continuity as ordinary common sense supposes.
why_it_mattered: Berkeley treats this need for a perpetual perceiver as itself a proof of God's existence, tightly binding his metaphysics of perception to natural theology.
historical_origin: Set out across the Principles and Dialogues; popularly immortalized in Ronald Knox's limerick and its reply, which Russell quotes in full.
examples: The Knox limerick: 'There was a young man who said, \"God / Must think it exceedingly odd ...\"' and its reply, 'I am always about in the Quad ... GOD.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly theological: continuity of the physical world becomes evidence for God's constant, universal perception.
